entries.sentence: Milder illness is usually managed at home.
entries.note: Most people recover at home without medical care.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes flu as an illness that comes on very quickly.
Typical features include a sudden high temperature, an aching body, tiredness, a dry cough, a sore throat and a headache.
Compared with a cold, flu leaves people exhausted and too unwell to carry on as normal.
Hospital leaflets that follow NHS advice describe a cold as building up gradually, with a runny nose, sneezing and watery eyes.
entries.note: Blended summary of NHS trust pages; specific trust not identified.

entries.sentence: Flu usually starts more suddenly, tends to be more severe and lasts longer than a cold.
Fever and body aches are more often part of flu.
Tiredness can linger after other symptoms ease, and a cough may last a week or so longer.
Because other viruses cause similar illnesses, the symptoms alone cannot prove that someone has flu.
entries.note: Symptoms alone cannot tell for sure.

entries.sentence: Flu is caused by influenza viruses.
The CDC describes four types, but only types A and B cause the seasonal epidemics seen in people.
entries.note: CDC: four types, A and B drive seasonal epidemics.

entries.sentence: Type A viruses are divided into subtypes such as H1N1 and H3N2, while type B viruses are split into two lineages.
Most experts think flu spreads mainly through droplets made when people with the infection cough, sneeze or talk.
The NHS says coughs and sneezes spread the germs, which can live on hands and surfaces for 24 hours.
Touching a contaminated surface and then the face is thought to be a less common route.
The CDC says the virus can be found in most infected people from one day before symptoms start and for five to seven days after they become ill.
People are most contagious during the first three days of the illness.
Clinicians often diagnose flu from the typical symptoms, and a swab test can confirm it.
Other viruses cause a similar illness, so symptoms alone cannot settle the question.
Quick tests exist, although some are less accurate than laboratory tests.
The CDC says most people can recover from flu at home without medical care.
One NHS hospital leaflet describes flu in otherwise healthy people as unpleasant but usually self-limiting, with recovery within 2 to 7 days.
entries.note: Blended summary quoting a trust leaflet; specific trust not identified.

entries.sentence: Other NHS leaflets put recovery at about a week.
entries.note: Summary: most sources put recovery at about a week.

entries.sentence: They add that tiredness can last longer than the other symptoms.
Symptoms that become more severe or last longer than about a week are a reason to seek medical advice.
entries.note: NHS: urgent contact if no improvement after 7 days.

entries.sentence: Most people recover at home with rest, plenty of fluids and over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.
NHS hospital leaflets add that keeping warm and drinking enough water helps avoid dehydration.
entries.note: Summary: rest at home, keep warm, drink plenty of water.

entries.sentence: Antibiotics do not work on flu, because it is caused by a virus.
The NHS says aspirin should not be given to children under 16.
Antiviral medicines can be prescribed for people at high risk or who are very sick.
They work best when started early, within about two days of symptoms beginning.
The CDC says antiviral treatment matters most for people at high risk, and can make the difference between a milder illness and a very serious one that ends in hospital.
An NHS trust leaflet says antivirals are generally not recommended for otherwise healthy adults.
entries.note: Summary: another source says not recommended for otherwise healthy adults; origin not identified.

entries.sentence: Most flu passes without lasting problems, but complications happen.
entries.note: Most recover at home; complications listed by NHS.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists bronchitis, pneumonia, sinus and ear infections, and inflammation of the heart or brain.
UKHSA adds that flu can make existing health conditions worse and, in severe cases, lead to hospital admission or death.
Older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with long-term conditions such as asthma, diabetes or heart disease are at higher risk.
The CDC also says even healthy children and adults can become very ill with flu.
For urgent concerns, the NHS advises contacting NHS 111 or the GP the same day when the person is 65 or over, pregnant, or has a long-term condition or weakened immune system.
The same applies when someone feels very unwell or short of breath, or has not improved after 7 days.
Sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood are reasons to call 999 or go to A&E.
Annual flu vaccination is the main recommended protection, alongside regular handwashing and covering coughs and sneezes.
UKHSA says the vaccine is updated every year because the flu virus changes.
UKHSA's guide to the autumn 2026 programme lists pregnant women, children, people aged 65 and over, and people in clinical risk groups among those eligible.
It also includes residents of long-stay care homes, close contacts of people with a weakened immune system, and some frontline social care workers.
The clinical risk groups include chronic respiratory disease such as asthma and COPD, chronic heart disease, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, diabetes and a weakened immune system.
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland follow their own health departments' guidance.
entries.note: Summary noted the UKHSA vaccine update says so; attributed to the blog/vaccine update.
